title: Circularity is moving from an environmental aspiration toward a resource-security, repair, resilience, and recurring-revenue strategy
source_unit: World Economic Forum and Bain & Company, The Resilience-to-Growth Circularity Playbook for Industrial Solutions and Manufacturing
geography: Industrial Solutions and Manufacturing executives across seven regions and ten industries, including a 94-person IS&M subgroup

observations.period: June 2026 executive survey; current and three-year circularity importance

denominator.unit: senior executives surveyed across ten industries and seven regions; IS&M subgroup n=94

current_importance.unit: percent of executives saying circularity is important or very important to their organization today

three_year_importance.unit: percent expecting circularity to be important or very important within three years

embedded_strategy.value: two-thirds report circular strategies embedded across one or more divisions or fully integrated into core strategy

execution_gap.value: cost, operational complexity, limited material visibility, immature secondary markets, fragmented ecosystems, and linear governance constrain scale

observations.method: WEF and Bain executive survey with 430 senior executives, including 94 leading Industrial Solutions and Manufacturing organizations, supplemented by company examples and playbook synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is an executive perspective sample rather than a representative census of firms; stated importance and strategy integration do not establish investment, material recovery, profitability, or environmental outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Industrial Solutions and Manufacturing executives, business units, suppliers, customers, repair and remanufacturing networks, and secondary-material markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Circularity may rise as a strategic label without changing production volumes, labor conditions, product affordability, or material throughput; some linear processes remain efficient or necessary in specific contexts.

observations.period: 2026; circularity's revenue, cost, and resource-security potential

denominator.unit: IS&M executives in the Circularity for Competitiveness and Resilience Executive Survey

revenue_potential.unit: percent expecting circular activities to contribute at least 20% of revenue at full potential

operating_cost_reduction.unit: percent expecting circularity to reduce operating costs at full potential

resource_security.unit: percent saying circularity could substantially address resource security if scaled

virgin_material_pressure.unit: percent likely or extremely likely to pursue circularity because of rising cost or reduced availability of virgin materials

observations.method: WEF and Bain sector survey asking IS&M executives about the full potential of circular models, resource security, costs, and revenues.
observations.uncertainty: Full-potential estimates are expectations, not realized revenue shares or cost reductions; they depend on market design, customer demand, secondary-material quality, financing, and execution.
observations.subgroup: Industrial machinery, equipment, manufacturing, service, refurbishment, remanufacturing, and resource-recovery businesses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Circular business models can create recurring revenue and resilience while also requiring upfront capital, new skills, reverse logistics, and potentially higher service or product prices.

denominator.unit: IS&M executive survey subgroup, with report-level industrial supply-chain context

critical_material_visibility.unit: percent of companies with a clear picture of exposure to critical raw materials and rare-earth elements

material_restrictions.unit: global critical-mineral import and export restrictions enacted in 2025 according to the report's cited context

rare_earth_supply_coverage.unit: share of 2035 demand covered by remaining global rare-earth and graphite supplies if supply from the dominant geography were disrupted, under the report's cited scenario

margin_pressure.value: average gross margins in the referenced IS&M context declined from 32% to 27% over the 15 years to 2024

observations.method: WEF and Bain survey combined with cited trade, material-concentration, margin, and supply-risk context; scenario values are retained as reported rather than treated as forecasts.
observations.uncertainty: The critical-material scenario depends on assumptions about demand, substitution, recycling, trade, and dominant-geography disruption; restrictions and margin context do not prove circularity would solve supply risk.
observations.subgroup: Manufacturers dependent on steel, aluminium, copper, nickel, lithium, graphite, rare earths, and concentrated global supply chains.
observations.counterinterpretation: Material restrictions can prompt substitution, diversification, and innovation; critical-material exposure differs sharply by product, geography, inventory, contracts, and recovery capability.

observations.period: 2026; circularity as repair, service, and installed-base strategy

denominator.unit: WEF/Bain circularity playbook framework for industrial products and equipment already in use

installed_base_route.value: repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing, modernization, leasing, rental, as-a-service, and end-of-life recovery are identified as routes to extend use and recover value

customer_capex_route.value: customers seeking to delay capital expenditure and prolong equipment life can align with service-led circular propositions

policy_enabler.unit: percent of IS&M executives naming regulation and policy as key enablers for their circular journey

three_step_route.value: quantify risk and value, codify high-value circular moves, and amplify through governance, data, partnerships, and finance

observations.method: WEF/Bain playbook synthesis of executive survey findings, industrial examples, and a three-step implementation framework.
observations.uncertainty: The framework describes potential value routes rather than demonstrating uptake, product-level durability, repair access, worker outcomes, customer savings, or reduced material extraction.
observations.subgroup: Equipment owners, manufacturers, repair workers, service providers, consumers of durable goods, regulators, financiers, and material-recovery systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Extending product life can reduce replacement demand but may delay adoption of safer or more efficient technologies; service models can improve access while increasing dependence on manufacturers and data platforms.

related_sources.claim: WEF Chief Sustainability Officers' Outlook provides complementary transition, adaptation, AI-resource, and resilience-capital context.
IEA World Energy Investment provides complementary energy and material-transition investment context.
OECD waste and resource-productivity work provides complementary policy and material-circularity context.

boundary: This record adds a circularity, resource-security, repair, and industrial-market route across supply-chain volatility, critical materials, installed equipment, recurring revenue, operating costs, regulation, and resilience. It uses a WEF/Bain executive survey and strategy synthesis, not verified circular flows, consumer repair access, product prices, worker outcomes, material substitution, causal profitability, or proof that circularity produces equitable environmental gains.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official WEF Circularity Playbook page and linked PDF were retrieved and reviewed for executive sample, circularity importance, revenue and cost expectations, critical-material exposure, supply-chain context, installed-base routes, policy enablers, and implementation framework.
